title: Henry VI at The Public with NAATCO #shakespeare #naatco #thepublicthe...
transcript: This all-Asian-American production of the relatively obscure Shakespeare trilogy of Henry VI is epic in multiple senses. Performed in four acts across two performances with a total run time of almost six hours, it follows a series of territorial and political conflicts under King Henry VI’s reign. If you're not familiar with the play, I'd recommend taking advantage of the provided act-by-act synopsis because there are a ton of characters, and six hours is a long time to spend being confused. I honestly spent most of Act 1 getting my bearings on who's who and settling into the intricate vocabulary this play offers. The initial mental investment pays off, though, and the rest of the play unfolds like a chess match. Some players die off unexpectedly, as others who were lying dormant slide in opportunistically. The entire ensemble is strong, though I was particularly impressed by Rajesh Bose as the Duke of York and Teresa Avia Lim as Queen Margaret, who feels like a more consequential character than her husband, whose name adorns the title of this play. Most of the other characters aren't afforded as much development simply due to their limited amount of time being alive, but they all contribute to something greater than the sum of its parts. I'm not generally drawn to Shakespeare's histories compared to his comedies or tragedies, and I'm still pretty indifferent about Henry VI as a play, but this production is quite strong. It illuminates the fickle nature of alliances and the pervasive or even contagious nature of violent ambition, though the overarching themes of greed, division, and catastrophically poor leadership aren't as sharply conveyed in the play itself as they are in some other Shakespeares. The exceptional length is not only intimidating, but feels unnecessary from a thematic standpoint — it's only the vast number of plot points that demand such an extensive run time. However, the scale of this play makes for an undeniably epic undertaking by this formidable cast. Between the performances, the sound design, and the staging, especially the stage combat, pretty much everything clicks. The only element that perplexed me was the costuming, which reads as equestrian meets retrofuturism meets bedding. I did appreciate how it took on a mangled and mutated look in Part 2, reflecting the civil strife and breakdown of leadership depicted. Overall, this production couldn't quite turn the play into a prince, but its shortcomings were mostly in the play itself. With that, two more Playbills for my collection.
reasoning: Reviewer praises the production strongly (performances, staging, stage combat) while remaining indifferent to the play itself and critiquing the length and costuming. Net signal is a recommendation of the production with clear caveats.
